articles.title: Respect online, and in the room

body.support:
Group chats and class talks have one thing in common: people. People react to *how* you say things.

**Online, tone gets lost.** People can't hear your voice. “ok.” can sound angry. So read your message again before you send it.

**Keep it safe**

- Don't share other people's photos or messages without asking.
- Keep your address and passwords private.
- If someone is being mean, don't join in. Screenshot it, block, and **report** it.
- Tell an adult you trust. You can also report to **eSafety**.

**Keep it respectful**

- Disagree with the *idea*, not the *person*.
- Say “I think…” not “You're wrong.”

**Good discussions**

- **Take turns.**
- **Listen.** Think about what they mean.
- **Add to ideas.** “Adding to what Jess said…”
- **Ask questions.** “Why do you think that?”
- **Bring others in.** “Sam, what do you think?”

Respect doesn't mean agreeing. It means everyone gets a say.
body.core:
Group chats, comment sections and class discussions have one thing in common: people. And people react to *how* you say things, not just *what* you say.

**Online, tone gets lost.** Face to face, people hear your voice and see your face. In a text, they don't. “ok.” can sound angry. A joke can sound like an insult. So read your message again before you send it. Ask: *how would this sound to them?*

**Keep it safe**

- Don't share other people's photos, screenshots or private messages without asking.
- Keep your own details private, like your address, phone number and passwords.
- If someone is being hurtful, don't pile on. Screenshot it, block, and **report** it to the platform.
- If it's serious and the platform doesn't help, you can report it to **eSafety** (esafety.gov.au). Tell an adult you trust, too.

**Keep it respectful**

- Disagree with the *idea*, not the *person*.
- Use *I*: “I see it differently, because…”
- Think about who's reading. It might be your teacher, your boss or your whole team.

**Discussions that work.** Whether it's a group chat about a project or a class discussion, the same rules help:

- **Take turns.** Let people finish.
- **Listen actively.** Focus on what the person means, not what you'll say next.
- **Build on ideas.** “Adding to what Jess said…”
- **Ask questions.** “What makes you think that?”
- **Bring others in.** “Sam, what do you reckon?”

Respect isn't about agreeing with everyone. It's about making it safe for everyone to have a say.
body.extend:
Group chats, comment threads and class discussions all depend on people working together. How a message is expressed shapes how it's received.

**Tone in digital text.** Online, readers lose the cues of voice, face and body language. A short reply (“ok.”) can read as hostile, and sarcasm is easily misread. Before sending, reread your message from the reader's point of view.

**Safe practice**

- Don't share others' images, screenshots or private messages without consent.
- Protect personal information: address, phone number, passwords and location.
- If someone is targeted, don't amplify it. Keep evidence (screenshots), block, and **report** to the platform.
- Serious cyberbullying that a platform doesn't deal with can be reported to the **eSafety Commissioner**. Involve a trusted adult.

**Respectful disagreement**

- Challenge the *idea*, not the *person*.
- Use “I” statements and give reasons: “I see it differently, because…”
- Consider your audience. Work and study chats are professional spaces.

**Conventions of discussion.** Productive discussion, online or face to face, relies on shared conventions:

- **Turn-taking:** let people finish, and keep contributions concise.
- **Active listening:** focus on the speaker's meaning, and check you've understood (“So you're saying…?”).
- **Building on ideas:** connect your point to others' (“Adding to Jess's point…”).
- **Questioning:** ask open questions that move the discussion forward (“What would that look like?”).
- **Inclusion:** invite quieter members in.

Respect isn't agreement. It's what makes it safe for everyone to contribute.

caseStudies.title: Cyberbullying reports surge

body.support:
In February 2025, **eSafety** shared new numbers. It's the government team that helps keep people safe online.

In **2024**, it got **2,978** reports of young people being bullied online. That was **25%** more than the year before.

In five years, reports went up by **more than 450%**.

**1,385** reports were about kids aged **13 and under**. That's almost half.

These are only the reports made to eSafety. Some people tell a school. Some tell no one.

It asked us all to be kind online.
body.core:
Each February, Australia marks **Safer Internet Day**. In 2025, **eSafety** used the day to share new numbers. It also asked people to be kinder online.

**eSafety** is the government's online safety team. People can go to it when an app won't help.

In **2024**, eSafety got **2,978** real reports of young people being bullied online. That was **25%** more than the year before.

In five years, reports had gone up by **more than 450%**.

It's not just teens. **1,385** reports, or **46%**, were about kids aged **13 and under**.

These numbers only count reports made to eSafety. They don't count ones made just to an app or a school. They don't count the ones nobody reported.

eSafety can step in when an app won't take down serious bullying. But the best fix starts sooner. It starts with what each of us posts, shares or calls out.
body.extend:
Each February, Australia marks **Safer Internet Day**. In February 2025, the **eSafety Commissioner** released new complaint data alongside a call for kindness online.

In **2024**, eSafety received **2,978** valid complaints about cyberbullying of young people, a rise of **25%** on the previous year. Over five years, complaints had grown by **more than 450%**.

The figures also showed how young many targets are. **1,385** complaints, or **46%**, involved children aged **13 and under**.

The data has limits. It counts only complaints made to eSafety. It doesn't capture problems reported only to platforms or schools, or never reported at all. A rise in complaints may also reflect more awareness of where to report, as well as more bullying.

eSafety can act when platforms fail to remove serious cyberbullying. But prevention depends on everyday choices: what people post, share, ignore or challenge.

teacher.overview: Students learn safe and respectful digital practice (tone in text, privacy, not sharing others' content, reporting) and the etiquette and conventions of discussion (turn-taking, active listening, building on ideas, questioning, including others). They analyse a made-up project group chat, sort and rewrite messages, build a discussion toolkit, and take part in a structured small-group discussion with roles. The case study is eSafety's February 2025 release: 2,978 valid cyberbullying complaints in 2024, up 25%, and more than 450% over five years.
prep: Know your school's wellbeing and reporting process. This topic can prompt disclosures; have a plan to follow up privately.
Choose a discussion question for the Do it that matters to students but isn't personal (e.g. a school rule, a local issue, phones at work).
Optional: role cards for leader, timekeeper, note-taker and observer.
Have eSafety's young people page ready to show.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** people can't hear your voice or see your face, so short replies or jokes can be misread. Don't pile on; screenshot; block; report to the platform; tell a trusted adult; report serious cases to eSafety. Take turns, listen actively, build on ideas, ask questions, bring others in.

**Group chat:** 1 respectful (clear, gives options); 2 rude (attacks the person); 3 respectful (builds on Mia's idea); 4 respectful (brings Sam in); 5 unsafe (shares a private message without consent); 6 respectful (calls it out calmly and refocuses).

**Sort:** Ali — respectful; “useless” — rude; Mel's address — unsafe; disagree with reason — respectful; ignore Kai — rude; sleeping photo — unsafe.

**Case study:** cyberbullying complaints to eSafety are rising fast (2,978 in 2024, up 25%; more than 450% over five years), and many involve children 13 and under. They don't show cases reported only to platforms or schools, or never reported. A bystander can refuse to share or react, check in privately with the target, call it out calmly, keep evidence and report it.

realityCheck: **Students may know the people in a story.** Keep examples made-up, and steer away from naming real classmates or chats.
**Disclosures happen.** Follow your school's process, and follow up privately.
**Rewrites can get sarcastic.** Model one that's genuinely respectful but still says the hard thing.
**Discussions need structure.** Roles and a timer make quieter students more likely to speak.
**Works in a real class:** yes, and the toolkit is useful well beyond this course.

levels.extend: Adds etiquette and constructive to the vocabulary, a quiz question on discussion versus debate, the limits of the eSafety data, and Level Ups on discussion, debate and active listening.
